content:
Caitlin Manno, Assistant Arts & Life Editor • November 22, 2026

Guests fill BoCo Boba as SLU theological studies professor Grant Kaplan prepares to speak on Oct. 26.

The Grand Center Arts District hosted an event exploring the history of Saint Louis University’s exorcism on Oct. 26. It was held at BoCo Boba and featured panelists John Waide, a retired SLU archivist, and  Grant Kaplan, a SLU professor of theological studies. Filled with SLU students and faculty, the cafe’s seating became standing room only. 

The event began with a detailed examination of the events that transpired in 1949 to a teenage boy known as “Robbie.”  Waide described Robbie’s origins in Washington D.C. and close relationship to St. Louis family member “Aunt Tillie” who introduced him to the Ouija board. Upon her death, Robbie allegedly used a Ouija board to contact her which is suspected to have led to demonic possession.

Waide discussed the odd things that began to happen in Robbie’s life after this such as scratches appearing on Robbie’s skin and items around the house shaking or moving randomly on their own. Robbie was taken to a doctor, psychologist, psychiatrist, Lutheran minister and then a Catholic parish to try and resolve the strange things that were occurring. 

Eventually, Robbie’s family decided to try finding answers in St. Louis where they met with SLU faculty the Rev. Raymond Bishop, the Rev. Laurence Kenny and SLU President the Rev. Paul Reinert, with Bishop in particular caring for Robbie’s case.

Bishop contacted the Rev. William Bowdren, who was the pastor of St. Francis Xavier College Church, and together they asked St. Louis Archbishop Joseph Ritter if they could perform the formal rite of exorcism, to which Ritter agreed.

Waide highlighted how frequently Robbie would be visited by Bishop, Bowdern and other Jesuits. Robbie exhibited increasingly odd behavior such as intense strength, disturbing screams, and speaking in tongues. Strange marks also appeared on Robbie’s body including a devil on his leg and the word “Hell,” on his chest.

On April 18, 1949, at Alexian Brothers Hospital, Bowdern’s exorcism was reportedly successful, with Robbie claiming to have dreamed of St. Michael the Archangel having fought the devil and demons to free him.

Waide noted that Robbie went on to live a normal life after the possession and never experienced any similar troubles. Bishop’s diary on these events would later be used for the books and films.

 Kaplan focused on the broader element of how demonic possession is viewed in theology. He emphasized the distinction between the devil as a single being and demons as multiple forces active in the world.

He touched on the concept of demonic oppression as when experiencing fatigue, melancholy and a series of bad occurrences. This is separate from demonic possession where there’s a greater loss of control and changes in voice and movements.

 Kaplan discussed the potential existence of a spiritual realm and intersecting laws that the world abides by. He addressed how in history, everyday things could be attributed to supernatural forces, but overtime people began to view the causes as a result of a natural set of laws.

Then came a rise in reporting supernatural activity, both angelic and demonic, where sightings would seep into the secular world. He noted a rise in horror films and media around this time as well.

Kaplan spent a great deal of time talking about witch trials and how their depiction represented people’s fear of the unknown and unexplained. He provided examples of witches in the past who were accused of spells, violent acts and forming sororities of witches.

The public perception was that trials were held, mainly with involvement from Catholics and Lutherans. These were not actually church trials, but witch commission trials where committees were formed solely to persecute witches.

After each panelist’s section, the event shifted into a question and answer section, emcee’d by the Grand Center Arts District’s president and CEO Peg Weathers. The panelists faced questions about exorcisms and theology. 

During this Q&A session, the panelists occasionally turned to a Jesuit in the audience to hear his thoughts. Quang Tran, a Jesuit priest and assistant professor in SLU’s psychology department, emphasized the importance of looking beyond the demonic elements to the holy aspects.

“Most people look for the sensational aspect of the story, but they don’t dig deeper into the theology of it, the context of it and its relationship to faith,” Tran said. “This is not really about the devil. It’s really about the power of God, the power of prayer, the power of the church’s prayer to heal and the power of obedience.”

Many students were in attendance including freshman accounting major Noah Jacob, who felt this event helps distinguish the legend from the taboo.

“I think these sorts of topics have a way of being swept under the rug. No matter what you believed actually happened, the legend and adaptations of the event could have easily turned this event into a taboo subject,” Jacob said. “I think by acknowledging it and outlining the historical significance, it can help to separate the myth and legend from the record.”

At this event, Weathers told a story about the 50th anniversary of the exorcism when she had the opportunity to walk down the hallway where it was performed on the third floor of Verhaegen Hall. She noted how the room numbers skipped a room and she had a sense that she didn’t want to mess with whatever’s inside even if it is all been resolved now.
